# Start here {#quickstart}

You have a paper going out. Your code lives in a folder that made sense to you
six months ago. This chapter is the shortest path from that to something a
stranger can download, open and run.

::: {.tada-key}
Four passes over your project, roughly in this order: fix the **paths and file
types**, **archive** it and get a DOI, write the **README**, and **annotate**
the scripts. Then have a colleague try to run it before a reviewer does.
:::

## The pre-submission checklist {#quickstart-checklist}

This is TADA as a single list. Each item links to the chapter that explains it.

**Transferable** — [full chapter](#transferable)

- [ ] Every script is saved with a standard code extension (`.R`, `.py`, `.cpp`, …), not inside a `.docx` or `.pdf`
- [ ] No `setwd()` (R) or `os.chdir()` (Python) anywhere
- [ ] No absolute paths (`/Users/you/…`, `C:/Users/you/…`) — relative paths only
- [ ] Data, code and materials all live in **one** project directory
- [ ] You have opened the project from a clean start and it still runs

**Available** — [full chapter](#available)

- [ ] Code is deposited in an immutable repository that mints a persistent identifier (Zenodo, Figshare, …)
- [ ] You have the DOI, and it is **cited in the manuscript text and reference list**
- [ ] If you developed on GitHub, you made a release and linked it to Zenodo — GitHub alone is not an archive

**Documented** — [full chapter](#documented)

- [ ] A `README.md` (or `README.txt`) sits at the top of the project
- [ ] It names the manuscript, the authors, a contact address, and any funders
- [ ] It lists software **and version** (e.g. R v4.3.3) and key packages **and versions** (e.g. ggplot2 v3.5.1)
- [ ] It states the licence
- [ ] It says where the data are (ideally with their own DOI)
- [ ] It says what each file is, what order to run things in, what the code needs and what it produces
- [ ] It flags anything slow or resource-hungry
- [ ] A licence is actually attached to the deposit

**Annotated** — [full chapter](#annotated)

- [ ] Code is broken into labelled chunks
- [ ] Each chunk says *what* it does, *why*, and *which* result it produces
- [ ] Signposts point at the manuscript ("produces Figure 3B", "Table 2, column 4")

**Before you submit** — [full chapter](#code-review)

- [ ] Someone else has run the whole thing from the archived files and it worked
- [ ] `set.seed()` / `random.seed()` is set before anything stochastic

::: {.tada-tip}
The single highest-value check on this page: **download your own archived
deposit into a fresh, empty folder on a different machine, and run it.** Almost
every reproducibility failure in the literature would have been caught by this.
:::

## A project layout that works {#quickstart-layout}

Wiki guidance, following the folder-and-file conventions recommended for
reviewable code. The point is not this exact tree — it is that the ordering and
purpose of everything is obvious without asking you.

```
my-project/
├── README.md                 <- start here: what this is, how to run it
├── LICENSE                   <- how others may use the code
├── my-project.Rproj          <- or a Python virtual environment
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                  <- never edited by any script
│   │   └── caterpillars_2024.csv
│   └── processed/            <- written by 01_, read by 02_
│       └── caterpillars_clean.csv
├── R/                        <- or scripts/, or src/
│   ├── 01_clean_data.R
│   ├── 02_fit_models.R
│   └── 03_make_figures.R
├── functions/                <- helpers sourced by the scripts above
│   └── utils.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    └── models/               <- saved model objects for slow fits
```

Two conventions are doing most of the work here:

1. **Numbered scripts.** A reader knows the order to run things in without
   being told. `01_`, `02_`, `03_`.
2. **`data/raw/` is read-only.** Cleaning writes to `data/processed/`. Raw data
   is never modified or overwritten by a script, so a botched cleaning step can
   never destroy the original.

## The three mistakes that break other people's runs {#quickstart-mistakes}

| Mistake | Why it breaks | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `setwd("C:/Users/ed/Desktop/analysis")` | The path exists on exactly one computer | An RStudio project or a Python virtual environment in the project folder, plus `here()` / `pyprojroot` |
| Code shared as a `.pdf` or `.docx` | Copy-pasting silently mangles apostrophes, quotes, and whitespace, and drags in line numbers and headers | Save as `.R` / `.py` |
| No `set.seed()` before a simulation or MCMC run | Results change every run, so nobody can tell a real mismatch from noise | Set a seed at the top of each independently-runnable section |

::: {.tada-warn}
The `.pdf`/`.docx` problem is nastier than it looks. The characters that get
substituted — curly apostrophes for straight ones, non-breaking spaces — produce
errors that are hard to see and slow to fix, because the code *looks* right.
:::

## A README you can fill in during a coffee break {#quickstart-readme}

Copy [`templates/README-template.md`](templates/README-template.md) into your
project and replace the angle-bracketed parts. The
[Documented](#documented-readme) chapter explains each field and why it is
there.

## What happens next {#quickstart-next}

If your target journal has a **data editor**, someone will check your deposit
against something close to the [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) — six stages, from
"is it archived with a licence" through to "do the results actually come out
the same". Reading that section tells you what the checks will be before
anyone runs them on you.

If your journal does not, the checks still matter — they just fall to you and
your co-authors. That is what [code review](#code-review) is for.
